title: MAGIC: Masked Multi-Path Contrast with Confidence-Gated Semantic Imputation
one_liner: MAGIC learns cluster semantics reliably before filling in missing data, using multiple paths that vote on meaning before completing views.
lead: When you cluster data from multiple sources and some views are missing, the usual approach fails: imputing (guessing) the missing data early triggers cascading errors, while trying to align views directly is unreliable when they rarely overlap. MAGIC flips the order: it first learns what the true clusters mean by building multiple correlated paths that vote on the answer, only then it carefully fills in the missing pieces using those learned cluster meanings.

problem.h2: Multi-view clustering breaks when data is incomplete
paras: Imagine you have customer profiles with three types of information: purchase history, browsing behavior, and survey responses. For some customers all three are there; for others, one or two are missing. The goal is to group customers into distinct types using all three views together.

A beginner tries the obvious: first fill in the missing pieces (predict what purchase history would look like for a customer with missing history), then cluster. But prediction errors compound—a bad guess for missing data gets locked in and corrupts all downstream learning.

Another beginner aligns the views directly, looking for patterns that match across all three sources. But when a customer is missing the survey response, that view cannot speak at all for them. The view that IS always present dominates; rarer views (like complete surveys) get drowned out.

callout.html: Learn what clusters mean FIRST before filling in missing data, using multiple paths that reach consensus.

steps.text: Gently add noise to each observed view separately; encode them into compressed number lists.
Create several correlated branches that each predict cluster assignment and reconstruction.
Hide one branch at a time (masked); the other branches vote on whether they agree. Record their confidence.
Use the learned cluster meanings to fill in missing data, but only if confidence is high enough.
Aggregate soft cluster assignments across views, assign each point to its strongest cluster.

paras: Instead of imputing first (guessing missing data early), MAGIC learns cluster semantics (what the clusters actually mean) on the data that IS present, then uses those learned meanings to fill in gaps safely.
object.object: order of learning: semantics before imputation

hidden.h2: Confidence: How sure is the agreement?
hidden.name: Consensus confidence across paths
paras: When multiple paths predict a cluster assignment, they don't always agree. Confidence measures how aligned those paths are—how many of them picked the same cluster, and how strongly. High confidence means the cluster meaning is trustworthy; low confidence means the prediction is fragile and we should not transfer it into missing data.

MAGIC estimates confidence by masking (hiding) one path at a time and checking if the remaining paths still vote the same way. High consensus confidence across masked trials means the cluster meaning holds up under change and is worth using to fill gaps.

heat.caption: Darker means higher agreement across multiple prediction paths; highlighted paths show consensus.

reads.html: If five out of six paths agree a customer is Type A, confidence is high; we can safely use that meaning to predict their missing survey. If only two out of six agree, confidence is low; we fall back to copying the nearest neighbor instead.

The paper uses consensus voting across the multiple prediction heads (paths) to measure how calibrated the cluster assignment is. Views with higher consensus drive the soft assignment; views with lower consensus are downweighted, reducing dominance of frequently-observed views.

mechanism.h2: Why learning semantics first prevents cascading errors
paras: When a wrong guess about missing data flows into clustering, it corrupts everything downstream. But a cluster semantic (the meaning of Type A, Type B, Type C) learned from observed data only is stable. Once you know what Type A looks like in dimensions that ARE observed, you can safely ask: what would a Type A customer's missing survey responses look like?

MAGIC enforces this by building multiple paths (several branches predicting cluster assignment and reconstruction in parallel). Each path sees the same observed data but encodes it slightly differently (via light augmentation). If all paths agree on which cluster a point belongs to, their consensus is strong—the semantics are clear. The paper masks each path (hides it) in turn and checks: do the other paths still vote the same way? If yes, confidence is high. This masked consensus is more reliable than a single path's prediction because it forces paths to reach agreement before the model even sees what semantics work best.

Once semantics are learned with high confidence, semantic transfer fills the gaps: transfer the learned Type-A pattern only where confidence is high; elsewhere, use a structure-preserving fallback (copy the nearest neighbor's structure) to avoid propagating low-confidence guesses.

stages.s: Observed data from multiple views (some views missing for some points)
Encode each view separately; build correlated prediction paths
Mask one path at a time; measure consensus confidence of others
Learn cluster semantics calibrated by consensus confidence
Transfer learned semantics to fill gaps (only high confidence); use fallback otherwise
Complete multi-view data with learned cluster structure

math.words: The learning goal is to minimize the prediction error across all paths while enforcing agreement under masking. When one path is hidden (masked), the other paths should still predict the same cluster. A weighted blend of reconstruction error (how well we predict observed data) and masked-consensus error (how well remaining paths agree when one is hidden) drives training. Once consensus confidence is high, semantic transfer fills missing values guided by that confidence score.
math.equation: L = L_consensus(C, C_hat) + lambda * L_consistency(X, X_hat) + gamma * L_confidence(conf_scores)
symbols: sum of disagreement between predicted cluster C and target cluster C_hat across all paths
reconstruction error: how well the predicted data X_hat matches observed data X
penalty for low confidence when imputing; high confidence scores are encouraged
weight controlling how much reconstruction error matters
weight controlling how much confidence in imputation matters

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a customer's purchase history and survey are observed, but browsing behavior is missing.
Consensus confidence = 2 high paths agreeing / 3 total = 0.67 → Transfer Type-A semantics to fill browsing.
Now hide Path 1; Paths 2+3 still predict: Path 2 = Type A (confidence 0.85), Path 3 = Type B (0.4).
Paths still agree mostly (Path 2 strong), so masked consensus penalty is low → training keeps this semantic structure.

If instead all paths had disagreed even without masking, confidence would be low, and the model would fall back to copying a similar customer's browsing instead of transferring fragile Type-A semantics.

math.note: The consensus loss trains multiple paths to vote together; masking forces agreement to be stable; confidence scores gate whether semantics are transferred or fallback to copying used instead.

items.b: Consensus can be misleading if all paths see the same bias.
items.html: If all prediction paths are initialized the same way or trained on the same noisy view, they may agree for the wrong reason. MAGIC mitigates this with light augmentation (different noise per view), but in extreme cases (e.g., one view is always extremely noisy), all paths can still agree on a bad cluster assignment.

items.b: Confidence score inflation in early training.
items.html: In the first few training steps, before semantics are well-learned, paths may randomly agree by chance. MAGIC's masked consensus helps, but early-stage imputation can still be unreliable. The paper handles this by warming up: only using high-confidence semantics after a certain number of training steps.

items.b: Structure-preserving fallback can propagate rare-view bias.
items.html: When confidence is low and the model falls back to copying the nearest neighbor, it can still amplify the dominance of frequently-observed views. If views 1 and 2 are always present but view 3 is rare, neighbors are found using views 1 and 2, and the fallback copies their structure, not view 3's.

The paper shows via ablation that both masked consensus and confidence-gated imputation are necessary. Removing either one degrades performance, confirming that the combination (not just one piece) is what prevents cascading errors.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a synthetic three-view clustering task where one view is always present, one is present 50 percent of the time, and one is present 20 percent of the time (simulating real-world imbalance). Implement two methods: (1) naive imputation followed by K-means clustering, (2) MAGIC's approach. Measure cluster purity (what fraction of each cluster's members are truly the same type) and normalized mutual information (how much the learned clusters match the ground truth). MAGIC should maintain high purity even at high missingness (e.g., 30–50 percent of entries missing) by avoiding cascading errors; naive imputation should degrade sharply.
demo.metric_eq: purity = (sum of max count per cluster per class) / total points; robustness = purity at 50% missingness minus purity at 10% missingness (MAGIC should be small, naive should be large)
demo.closing: The demo must show that MAGIC's purity stays stable across different missingness levels, while naive imputation collapses as missingness increases—proving that learning semantics before imputation prevents cascading errors.
